extracted.intended_audience: beginner Korean learners, travelers, and general readers curious about the Korean language
extracted.subtask_description: A broad introductory guide covering Korean history, dialects, writing system (Hangul/Hanja), pronunciation, grammar (word order, honorifics), vocabulary, and practical learning advice for beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn Hangul first
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be much easier and faster if you first learn the alphabet (Hangul/Hangeul). Many people can learn basic Hangul in about 1 hour; many native English speakers can learn the alphabet in about 1-2 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning Hangul helps you pronounce words more accurately and understand what you hear more easily. You can learn to speak Korean without learning Hangul, but Hangul accelerates progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best way to learn: basic grammar, phrases, and interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to learn Korean is to learn some basic grammar and phrases and start interacting with people in Korean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with basic grammar and phrases; then practice by interacting with native speakers to develop speaking ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic word order is subject-object-verb (SOV)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic word order for Korean sentences is subject-object-verb. The word order is flexible, and the verb is often the only word you need for the sentence to make sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners can start creating sentences quickly by focusing on verb placement and simple grammar patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation: Korean is phonetic and has no tones
rubrics_metrics.description: Korean is a phonetic language — you can sound out individual letters to make words. There are no tones in standard Korean, so pronunciation rules are generally simple and clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romanization is useful for approximating words into English but is not good for pronunciation; learning Hangul is preferred for accurate pronunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of honorifics and speech levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Koreans use honorifics and speech levels to show relationship between speaker and addressee. Use 존댓말 (jondaetmal) for polite speech toward older/higher-status people, 반말 (banmal) for informal speech with friends/younger people, and a neutral speech level for general situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose speech level based on relative age/status and closeness; honorifics are necessary when talking about or to someone of higher status or older age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard dialect recommendation for learners
rubrics_metrics.description: Seoul dialect is the standard version used in speeches and news reports in South Korea and is the language most Korean learners are learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can learn regional dialects if desired, but for beginners the suggestion is to learn the standard Seoul dialect first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialects and dialect divergence (Jeju notable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Korean has nine different dialects; Jeju Island's dialect is the most significantly different from standard Korean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that North and South Korean dialects and accents have diverged (influenced by Russian in the North and English in the South), affecting vocabulary and pronunciation; however, mutual understanding is generally possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hanja historical use and modern guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Hanja (Chinese characters) were used historically to write Korean; they were officially used until about 100 years ago. In South Korea Hanja still appears in some official documents and dictionaries; in North Korea Hanja has not been used since 1949.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learners should know Hanja exists and that many Korean words have Chinese origin, but Hanja is not essential for basic modern Korean literacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary composition: many loanwords and Chinese-origin words
rubrics_metrics.description: Korean vocabulary consists of native Korean words at its core but contains many words borrowed from Chinese and other languages (English, Russian, Japanese, German, Mongolian). Estimates of Chinese-origin words vary widely (30%–65%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a significant portion of vocabulary to be Sino-Korean; regional (North/South) differences affect which borrowed words are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: North vs South vocabulary and spelling differences
rubrics_metrics.description: North Korea has tried to replace many Chinese loanwords with native Korean words, resulting in vocabulary differences between North and South; pronunciation, spelling, and grammar have also diverged over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When learning, be aware that some words used in one country may not exist or be used differently in the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romanization is an approximation, not a pronunciation substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: Korean can be written in English letters following an official romanization system; it’s useful for approximating words into English, but it’s not good for pronunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer learning Hangul for pronunciation rather than relying on romanization systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: TOPIK as official proficiency test and practical requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The official test of the Korean language is the TOPIK. This test is often required to work at Korean companies or to obtain a visa in Korea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need Korean for professional or immigration reasons, prepare for and take TOPIK as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Institute of Korean Language as authoritative resource
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Institute of Korean Language does research and creates language policies; they provide a useful dictionary that also has audio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the institute's dictionary and resources for authoritative usage and pronunciation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: No grammatical gender but gender-specific vocabulary exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Technically there is no grammatical gender in Korean — words are not gendered like in French. However, there are gender-specific pronouns (그 for a man, 그녀 for a woman) and many vocabulary items that indicate gender (e.g., 오빠 oppa, 언니 eonni).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that gender is conveyed lexically rather than grammatically; choose words appropriately when you need to indicate gender.
